source_batch.unit_label: BRBL Module A unit 7: financial sector legislative reforms and the Financial Stability and Development Council

facts.statement: Why reforms were needed and the first Narasimham Committee (courseware): the financial system in India had many regulators, each with a separate mandate, producing fragmentation of legislation, regulation enforcement, overlapping jurisdictions and risk of regulatory arbitrage; a need was felt to rewrite and streamline financial sector laws and bring them in harmony with the requirements of a fast growing financial sector. Before reforms the banking sector suffered from financial repression such as extensive regulations, administered interest rates, directed credit programmes, weak banking structure and lack of proper risk management systems. The Narasimham Committee (Committee on the Financial System, CFS) was set up in August 1991 to examine all aspects of the structure, organisation, functions and procedures of the financial system and submitted its report in November 1991. Findings: the CRR and SLR kept by banks were very high (aggregating to 53.5 per cent at that time), which led to continuous loss in potential income and affected profitability; the Committee called the high SLR/CRR a tax on the banking system and recommended lowering it. Directed credit: the Committee criticised directed lending to priority sector as overlooking qualitative aspects of credit with no proper appraisal, no insistence on collateral and weak post credit supervision and monitoring. Interest subsidy: the Committee thought that interest subsidy offered in various schemes, especially government sponsored ones, was a loss of precious profits and timely credit was more important than subsidised interest. Other findings: opening of a large number of branches without considering viability, command and control stretched too far with weak inspection and audit leading to unreconciled inter-branch entries and frauds, deterioration in staff quality, and excessive bank credit to agriculture and small industry where the cost of administering loans was high.

Narasimham Committee II and the FSLRC (courseware): the Committee on Banking Sector Reforms (Narasimham Committee II) was set up in December 1997 to review the progress of implementation of financial sector reforms recommended by the CFS and submitted its report in April 1998. Major recommendations: strengthening of the banking system through capital adequacy measures including the concept of risk weights, higher risk weights where required and higher capital adequacy ratio; introduction of stringent asset quality norms (sticky advances guaranteed by the Government to be treated as NPA, interest subsidy for priority sector to be eliminated or introduced), the concept of asset reconstruction companies, strict income recognition and asset classification (IRAC) norms, and disclosure requirements. Many recommendations were implemented while some remain under consideration. After the report, between 1998 and 2011, reforms were introduced piecemeal, such as adherence to Basel 3 norms, enactment of the SARFAESI Act in 2002. After the Global Financial Crisis of 2008, the Financial Sector Legislative Reforms Commission (FSLRC), headed by Justice B.N. Srikrishna, was set up by the Ministry of Finance in March 2011 to review, simplify and rewrite the legal and institutional structures of the financial sector and submitted its report in March 2013. Its objectives included remedial measures for the banking policy, institutional structure, supervisory system and legislative and technological changes. Contours of the reforms: removal of the existing financial repression; creation of an efficient, productive and profitable financial sector; price discovery by the market and determination of interest rates; operational and functional autonomy; preparation for increasing competition; opening of the external sector in a calibrated manner; and promoting financial stability in the wake of domestic and external shocks. Sectors: banking sector, monetary policy, financial markets and the forex market.

Banking sector reforms: competition and market forces (courseware): the aim was a diversified, efficient and competitive financial system improving allocative efficiency through operational flexibility, improved financial viability and institutional strengthening. Reforms fall in six groups: competition enhancing measures, measures enhancing the role of market forces, prudential measures, institutional and legal measures, supervisory measures and technology related measures. Competition enhancing: operational autonomy to public sector banks and reduction of public ownership by allowing them to raise capital from the equity market up to 49 per cent of paid-up capital; transparent norms for entry of Indian private sector, foreign and joint venture banks and insurance companies, permission for foreign investment in the financial sector as FDI and portfolio investment; roadmap for presence of foreign banks; foreign banks permitted to operate through branches, a wholly owned subsidiary or a subsidiary with foreign investment up to a maximum of 74 per cent of paid-up capital; licensing of banks in the private sector and part divestment in public sector banks; differentiated banks and small finance banks; after the nationalisation of 14 large banks in 1969, introduction of greater competition in the 1990s with new private banks (HDFC, ICICI, UTI Bank, IDBI Bank), and NBFCs; migration to core banking solution; voluntary retirement scheme (2001); by 2008 bank balance sheets were stronger and NPAs had come down from a peak of about 12 per cent to slightly over 2 per cent. Measures enhancing the role of market forces: sharp reduction in pre-emption through reserve requirement, market determined pricing for government securities, disbanding of administered interest rates with few exceptions and enhanced transparency and disclosure norms; introduction of a pure inter-bank call money market, auction based repos, reverse repos for short-term liquidity management, improved payments and settlement mechanisms; dematerialisation and markets for securitised assets; and the Targeted Long Term Repo Operations Scheme under which banks borrow on tap at repo rates for periods up to 3 years for investing in specific sectors.

Prudential, institutional, supervisory and technology reforms (courseware): Prudential measures: international best practices and phased implementation of norms on risk-weighted capital adequacy, accounting, income recognition, provisioning and exposure. The SLR which was 38.5 per cent in 1991-92 was brought down to some 28 per cent in five years and the CRR brought down from 14 per cent to 10 per cent by 1997; CRAR of scheduled commercial banks introduced in 1992 stood at 14.2 per cent as at March 2022, remaining well above the regulatory requirement of 9.0 per cent; frameworks on countercyclical capital buffer, leverage ratio, liquidity coverage ratio, net stable funding ratio, guidelines on large exposures effective from 1 April 2019. Other prudential measures: risk management recognising components of risk and risk weights; lending, risk concentration, marked-to-market principle for investment portfolio; KYC and anti money laundering guidelines, introduction of Basel II/III guidelines, a capital charge for market risk, higher graded provisioning for NPAs, guidelines for ownership and governance, securitisation and debt restructuring mechanisms; IRAC norms; deregulation of credit processes and interest rate structure (the Reserve Bank no longer prescribes interest rates on fixed or time deposits and banks are free from any prescribed conditions of premature withdrawal). Institutional and legal measures: Lok Adalats, debt recovery tribunals, asset reconstruction companies and settlement advisory committees; SARFAESI Act, 2002; Credit Information Bureau (India) Limited (CIBIL); Clearing Corporation of India Limited (CCIL) as central counterparty for payment and settlement systems for fixed income securities and money market instruments; and the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016. Supervisory measures: Board for Financial Supervision as apex supervisory authority; CAMELS rating system, move towards risk-based supervision, consolidated supervision of financial conglomerates and strengthened off-site surveillance; recasting the role of statutory auditors and stronger internal control; corporate governance, due diligence on shareholders, fit and proper tests for directors; the Enhanced Access and Service Excellence (EASE) reforms agenda introduced by the Government in January 2018 for public sector banks. Technology measures: INFINET as the communication backbone, Negotiated Dealing System for screen-based trading in government securities, the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007, RTGS, NEFT, ECS, ATMs, mobile banking, internet banking, e-commerce, IMPS and UPI; a September 2020 circular requiring scheduled commercial banks and small finance banks to have IT systems for identification of NPAs; and the adoption of artificial intelligence, machine learning, robotics, digital banking, links with fintech companies and blockchain technology.

Reforms in monetary policy, money, government securities and capital markets (courseware): the twin objectives of monetary policy are maintaining price stability and ensuring availability of adequate credit to productive sectors of the economy to support growth. With increasing development of the financial market and greater liberalisation, use of broad money as an intermediate target has been de-emphasised and a multiple indicator approach adopted; emphasis has been put on development of multiple instruments to transmit liquidity and interest rate signals in the short-term in a flexible and bi-directional manner; interlinkage among markets (money, government security and forex) has been increased; instruments move from direct instruments (such as administered interest rates, reserve requirements, selective credit control) to indirect instruments (such as open market operations, purchase and repurchase of government securities) for the conduct of monetary policy. The Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF), operating through repo and reverse repo auctions, provides a corridor for short-term interest rate: LAF is the tool for both liquidity management and a signalling device for interest rate in the overnight market. On 8 April 2022 the Reserve Bank introduced the Standing Deposit Facility (SDF), which is the floor limit of the policy corridor while the Marginal Standing Facility (MSF) is the ceiling. Open market operations deal with overall market liquidity especially emanating from capital flows; the Market Stabilization Scheme (MSS) is an additional instrument to deal with enduring capital inflows without affecting the short-term liquidity management role of LAF. Money market reforms: deregulation of interest rates on call and other money market instruments from the late 1980s; introduction of Commercial Paper and Certificate of Deposit, exemption of inter-bank lending from reserve requirement, screen-based trading, rupee derivatives such as Interest Rate Swaps and Forward Rate Agreements, enlarging the repo market, and tri-party repo (Collateralised Borrowing and Lending Obligation (CBLO) replaced by Tri-party Repo from 10 August 2017). Repo and CBLO volumes rose as the call market became a pure inter-bank market. Government securities market: until the mid-1980s the government had been borrowing at sub-market rates through a captive market created by the SLR; reforms eliminated automatic monetisation of deficit through Ways and Means Advances, with G-secs, State Development Loans, Treasury Bills and Cash Management Bills auctioned by the Reserve Bank; since April 2006 the Reserve Bank does not participate in the primary G-sec market. Capital market: movement from the Controller of Capital Issues regime to free pricing and book-building with mandatory disclosures prescribed by SEBI, corporatisation of exchanges, screen based trading replacing open outcry, options and futures, rolling settlement replacing the 14-day settlement cycle and the Badla system, and dematerialisation with depositories.

Reforms in the forex market (courseware): reforms included adoption of a managed floating exchange rate arrangement, rationalisation of the structure of the market, introduction of a variety of products such as options and swaps, and gradual move towards capital account convertibility with intervention by the Reserve Bank. Liberalisation measures: authorised dealers permitted to initiate trading positions and borrow and invest in overseas markets subject to specifications and ratification by the bank Boards; banks permitted to fix interest rates on non-resident deposits and use derivative products for asset-liability management and fix overnight open position limits and gap limits subject to ratification by the Reserve Bank; exporters, Indians investing abroad and Foreign Institutional Investors permitted to avail of forward cover and enter into swap transactions without any limit subject to genuine underlying; FIIs and NRIs permitted to trade in exchange-traded derivative contracts subject to conditions; exchange earners allowed to maintain foreign currency accounts (EEFC). Before reforms the market was virtually non-existent: exchange earners had to surrender and purchase foreign exchange from the Reserve Bank at the reference rate, and trades were squared by the close of the day. After reforms there was introduction of a market based exchange rate regime, adoption of current account convertibility, relaxation on capital account, permission to run open positions, to invest abroad and retain foreign exchange, and hedging tools (derivatives), giving active and vibrant foreign exchange markets; the rupee is now effectively convertible for non-residents on capital account (courseware statement). Reforms are continuing, as seen in the State Bank of India Act amendments of 2007 and 2010 and the Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act, 2020 (courseware).

Financial Stability and Development Council (courseware): financial sector regulation is vital for a healthy and efficient financial system. The FSDC was constituted in December 2010 by the Government of India with the Finance Minister as the Chairman; it is not a statutory body. Regulators for various sectors: the Reserve Bank for commercial banks and NBFCs, SEBI for the capital market, IRDA for insurance and PFRDA for pension funds. The primary objective is to strengthen and institutionalise the mechanism for maintaining financial stability, promoting financial sector development and enhancing inter-regulatory coordination; coordination among regulators ensures better efficiency and avoids overlapping of functions. Composition: the Chairman is the Finance Minister; members include heads of financial sector regulators (RBI, SEBI, IRDAI and PFRDA), the Finance Secretary and/or Secretary, the Secretaries of the Department of Economic Affairs, Department of Financial Services, Revenue Department and Ministry of Information Technology, the Chairman of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India and the Chief Economic Adviser. Functions: to strengthen and institutionalise the mechanism for maintaining financial stability and development; monitoring of macro-prudential supervision of the economy including the functions of large financial conglomerates; enhancing inter-regulatory coordination; and focus on financial literacy and financial inclusion. Wings: the FSDC Sub-Committee (chaired by the Governor of the Reserve Bank, meets more often than the full Council, with all members of the Council and all four Deputy Governors of the Reserve Bank and the Additional Secretary DEA in charge as members); the Inter-regulatory Technical Group (IR-TG) set up in September 2011 and headed by the Executive Director in charge of Financial Stability at the Reserve Bank (meets once every two to three months); the Technical Group on Financial Inclusion and Financial Literacy (TGFIFL) set up in November 2011 and chaired by the Deputy Governor of the Reserve Bank in charge of financial stability; the Inter Regulatory Forum for monitoring Financial Conglomerates (IRF-FC) set up in August 2012, headed by the Deputy Governor of the Reserve Bank in charge of banking supervision with senior representatives of RBI, SEBI, IRDAI and PFRDA; the Working Group on resolution regime for financial institutions (the Reserve Bank constituted a High Level Working Group in January 2013 to examine the existing resolution framework against the key attributes of the Financial Stability Board); the Macro Financial Monitoring Group (MFMG), chaired by the Chief Economic Adviser and set up on 16 May 2012, which keeps track of macroeconomic and financial developments and provides early warning signals; the Early Warning Group set up in June 2012 and chaired by the Deputy Governor of the Reserve Bank in charge of Financial Markets; and the Crisis Prevention and Monitoring Framework (CPMF), which helps regulators identify and mitigate emerging threats to financial and macroeconomic stability and highlights the prevention aspect.

payload.title: Why reforms were needed and the first Narasimham Committee (1991)
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Problems before reform:** **many regulators with separate mandates**, **fragmented laws**, **overlapping jurisdictions** and **regulatory arbitrage**; a banking sector marked by **financial repression**: heavy **regulation**, **administered interest rates**, **directed credit**, a **weak structure** and **poor risk management**.

**Narasimham Committee I (Committee on the Financial System, CFS):** set up in **August 1991**, report in **November 1991**; the **first systematic attempt** at reforming the financial system.

- **High SLR and CRR:** together about **53.5 per cent** at the time; the Committee called this a **'tax on the banking system'** and recommended **lowering** it.
- **Directed credit:** priority sector lending without **appraisal, collateral or follow-up** hurt **loan quality**.
- **Interest subsidy:** **timely credit** matters more than **subsidised interest**; subsidies cost banks profit.
- **Other findings:** **too many unviable branches**, **over-stretched command and control** (weak inspection, **unreconciled inter-branch entries**, **frauds**), **poor staff quality**, and **high cost** of small agricultural and small industry loans.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The 1991 report set the direction for later bank reforms: lower reserve requirements, less direction and more commercial discipline.

payload.title: Narasimham Committee II and the FSLRC
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Narasimham Committee II (Committee on Banking Sector Reforms):** set up in **December 1997**, report in **April 1998**, to review the progress of the **CFS** recommendations. Main ideas:

- **Stronger capital:** **risk weights**, **higher weights where needed**, **higher CRAR**.
- **Asset quality:** **stringent norms**; **Government-guaranteed sticky advances** treated as **NPA**; **interest subsidy for priority sector** to be eliminated or restructured; **asset reconstruction companies**; **strict IRAC (income recognition, asset classification) norms** and **disclosure**.

**Piecemeal reforms 1998-2011:** adopting **Basel norms**, the **SARFAESI Act, 2002** and others.

**FSLRC (Financial Sector Legislative Reforms Commission):** set up by the **Ministry of Finance** in **March 2011** under **Justice B.N. Srikrishna** after the **2008 Global Financial Crisis**; report in **March 2013**. It aimed to **review, simplify and rewrite the legal and institutional structures** and covered **banking policy, institutional structure, supervisory system and legislative and technological changes**.

**Reform themes:** end **financial repression**; an **efficient, productive and profitable** sector; **market price discovery** and **market determined interest rates**; **operational autonomy**; **competition**; **calibrated opening to the external sector**; **financial stability**. Reforms were grouped by **banking, monetary policy, financial markets and forex**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Narasimham II moved from liberalisation to strengthening the system, and the FSLRC aimed at redesigning financial laws.

payload.title: Banking sector reforms: competition and market forces
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Aim:** a **diversified, efficient and competitive** system that improves **allocative efficiency**. **Six groups of reform:** **competition enhancing**, **market forces**, **prudential**, **institutional and legal**, **supervisory** and **technology**.

**Competition enhancing measures:**

- **Operational autonomy** for public sector banks and **raising equity** from the market (**up to 49 per cent of paid-up capital**, as the courseware says).
- **Transparent entry norms** for **private, foreign and joint venture banks and insurers**; **FDI and portfolio investment**.
- **Foreign banks** via **branches**, **wholly owned subsidiary** or a **subsidiary with up to 74 per cent foreign investment** (courseware).
- **New private banks** after **1991** (**HDFC, ICICI, UTI Bank, IDBI**), **differentiated and small finance banks**, **NBFCs**, **core banking migration** and **VRS (2001)**. By **2008** NPAs had fallen from **about 12 per cent** to **just over 2 per cent**.

**Measures enhancing market forces:** **sharp cuts in pre-emption through reserve requirements**; **market-determined pricing of government securities**; **disbanding of administered interest rates**; a **pure inter-bank call money market**; **auction based repos and reverse repos**; **dematerialisation** and **securitisation markets**; and **Targeted Long Term Repo Operations** (banks borrow **on tap** at the **repo rate** for **up to 3 years** for specific sectors).
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Competition and market pricing replaced administered rates and captive government borrowing.

payload.title: Prudential, institutional, supervisory and technology reforms
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Prudential:** phased adoption of **international best practice** on **capital adequacy**, **income recognition**, **classification and provisioning**; **SLR cut from 38.5 per cent (1991-92) to about 28 per cent in five years**; **CRR cut from 14 per cent to 10 per cent by 1997**; **CRAR introduced in 1992**; later **countercyclical buffer, leverage ratio, LCR, NSFR and large exposure norms (April 2019)**; **KYC and AML**, **Basel II and III**, a **market risk capital charge**, **graded NPA provisioning**, **ownership and governance rules**, **securitisation and debt restructuring**; **deregulated interest rates** and **premature withdrawal** conditions.

**Institutional and legal:** **Lok Adalats**, **debt recovery tribunals**, **asset reconstruction companies**, **SARFAESI Act 2002**, **CIBIL**, **CCIL** (central counterparty for fixed income and money market trades), the **Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code 2016**.

**Supervisory:** **Board for Financial Supervision** as apex body; **CAMELS rating**; **risk based supervision**; **consolidated supervision of conglomerates**; **off-site surveillance**; stronger **statutory audit and internal control**; **corporate governance and fit and proper tests**; the **EASE** programme (January 2018) for public sector banks.

**Technology:** **INFINET**, the **Negotiated Dealing System**, the **Payment and Settlement Systems Act 2007**, **RTGS, NEFT, ECS, ATMs, mobile and internet banking, IMPS and UPI**, plus **AI, machine learning, robotics, fintech tie-ups and blockchain**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Reserve requirements fell sharply, replaced by capital based discipline and market tools.

payload.title: Reforms in monetary policy and in the money, government securities and capital markets
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Monetary policy aims:** **price stability** and **adequate credit for productive sectors** to support growth. **Changes:** **broad money** was dropped as the intermediate target for a **multiple indicator approach**; **direct instruments** (**administered rates, reserve requirements, selective credit control**) gave way to **indirect instruments** (**open market operations**).

**Liquidity tools:**

- **Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF):** **repo and reverse repo auctions** form a **corridor** for the overnight rate and signal policy.
- **Standing Deposit Facility (SDF), 8 April 2022:** the **floor** of the policy corridor; the **Marginal Standing Facility (MSF)** is the **ceiling**.
- **Open market operations:** manage liquidity from **capital flows**.
- **Market Stabilization Scheme (MSS):** absorbs **enduring capital inflows** without disturbing LAF.

**Money market:** **interest rate deregulation** from the late **1980s**, **Commercial Paper and Certificates of Deposit**, **screen based trading**, **rupee swaps and forward rate agreements**, a wider **repo market**, and **tri-party repo** (**10 August 2017**, replacing **CBLO**).

**Government securities:** the **captive SLR market** gave way to **auctions**; **automatic monetisation** through **Ways and Means Advances** ended; since **April 2006** the Reserve Bank does **not** take part in the **primary market**.

**Capital market:** from the **Controller of Capital Issues** to **free pricing and book building**, **corporatised exchanges**, **screen trading**, **futures and options**, **rolling settlement replacing the 14-day cycle and Badla**, and **depositories**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: A policy corridor with a floor (SDF) and ceiling (MSF) keeps the overnight rate within a band.

payload.title: Reforms in the forex market
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Before reform:** the market was **virtually non-existent**; exchange earners had to **surrender and buy foreign exchange from the Reserve Bank** at the **reference rate** and trades were **squared by day end**.

**Reform measures:** a **managed floating exchange rate**; a rationalised market structure; **new products** (**options, swaps**); a gradual shift to **capital account convertibility** with **Reserve Bank intervention** as needed.

**Liberalisation:** authorised dealers may **take trading positions** and **borrow and invest overseas** (with Board ratification); banks may set **interest rates on non-resident deposits** and use **derivatives for asset-liability management** within **open position and gap limits**; **exporters, Indians investing abroad and FIIs** may take **forward cover and swaps** against a **genuine underlying**; **FIIs and NRIs** may trade **exchange traded derivatives**; exporters may keep **foreign currency accounts (EEFC)**.

**Result:** a **market-based exchange rate**, **current account convertibility**, relaxed **capital account**, ability to **hold open positions** and **retain foreign exchange**, and **hedging tools**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Forex reforms moved the market from surrender-and-sell control to a market in which participants hedge and trade.

items.title: Why reforms were needed and the first Narasimham Committee (1991)
items.core_explanation_md:
**Problems before reform:** **many regulators with separate mandates**, **fragmented laws**, **overlapping jurisdictions** and **regulatory arbitrage**; a banking sector marked by **financial repression**: heavy **regulation**, **administered interest rates**, **directed credit**, a **weak structure** and **poor risk management**.

**Narasimham Committee I (Committee on the Financial System, CFS):** set up in **August 1991**, report in **November 1991**; the **first systematic attempt** at reforming the financial system.

- **High SLR and CRR:** together about **53.5 per cent** at the time; the Committee called this a **'tax on the banking system'** and recommended **lowering** it.
- **Directed credit:** priority sector lending without **appraisal, collateral or follow-up** hurt **loan quality**.
- **Interest subsidy:** **timely credit** matters more than **subsidised interest**; subsidies cost banks profit.
- **Other findings:** **too many unviable branches**, **over-stretched command and control** (weak inspection, **unreconciled inter-branch entries**, **frauds**), **poor staff quality**, and **high cost** of small agricultural and small industry loans.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The 1991 report set the direction for later bank reforms: lower reserve requirements, less direction and more commercial discipline.

items.title: Narasimham Committee II and the FSLRC
items.core_explanation_md:
**Narasimham Committee II (Committee on Banking Sector Reforms):** set up in **December 1997**, report in **April 1998**, to review the progress of the **CFS** recommendations. Main ideas:

- **Stronger capital:** **risk weights**, **higher weights where needed**, **higher CRAR**.
- **Asset quality:** **stringent norms**; **Government-guaranteed sticky advances** treated as **NPA**; **interest subsidy for priority sector** to be eliminated or restructured; **asset reconstruction companies**; **strict IRAC (income recognition, asset classification) norms** and **disclosure**.

**Piecemeal reforms 1998-2011:** adopting **Basel norms**, the **SARFAESI Act, 2002** and others.

**FSLRC (Financial Sector Legislative Reforms Commission):** set up by the **Ministry of Finance** in **March 2011** under **Justice B.N. Srikrishna** after the **2008 Global Financial Crisis**; report in **March 2013**. It aimed to **review, simplify and rewrite the legal and institutional structures** and covered **banking policy, institutional structure, supervisory system and legislative and technological changes**.

**Reform themes:** end **financial repression**; an **efficient, productive and profitable** sector; **market price discovery** and **market determined interest rates**; **operational autonomy**; **competition**; **calibrated opening to the external sector**; **financial stability**. Reforms were grouped by **banking, monetary policy, financial markets and forex**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Narasimham II moved from liberalisation to strengthening the system, and the FSLRC aimed at redesigning financial laws.

items.title: Banking sector reforms: competition and market forces
items.core_explanation_md:
**Aim:** a **diversified, efficient and competitive** system that improves **allocative efficiency**. **Six groups of reform:** **competition enhancing**, **market forces**, **prudential**, **institutional and legal**, **supervisory** and **technology**.

**Competition enhancing measures:**

- **Operational autonomy** for public sector banks and **raising equity** from the market (**up to 49 per cent of paid-up capital**, as the courseware says).
- **Transparent entry norms** for **private, foreign and joint venture banks and insurers**; **FDI and portfolio investment**.
- **Foreign banks** via **branches**, **wholly owned subsidiary** or a **subsidiary with up to 74 per cent foreign investment** (courseware).
- **New private banks** after **1991** (**HDFC, ICICI, UTI Bank, IDBI**), **differentiated and small finance banks**, **NBFCs**, **core banking migration** and **VRS (2001)**. By **2008** NPAs had fallen from **about 12 per cent** to **just over 2 per cent**.

**Measures enhancing market forces:** **sharp cuts in pre-emption through reserve requirements**; **market-determined pricing of government securities**; **disbanding of administered interest rates**; a **pure inter-bank call money market**; **auction based repos and reverse repos**; **dematerialisation** and **securitisation markets**; and **Targeted Long Term Repo Operations** (banks borrow **on tap** at the **repo rate** for **up to 3 years** for specific sectors).
items.expanded_explanation_md: Competition and market pricing replaced administered rates and captive government borrowing.

items.title: Prudential, institutional, supervisory and technology reforms
items.core_explanation_md:
**Prudential:** phased adoption of **international best practice** on **capital adequacy**, **income recognition**, **classification and provisioning**; **SLR cut from 38.5 per cent (1991-92) to about 28 per cent in five years**; **CRR cut from 14 per cent to 10 per cent by 1997**; **CRAR introduced in 1992**; later **countercyclical buffer, leverage ratio, LCR, NSFR and large exposure norms (April 2019)**; **KYC and AML**, **Basel II and III**, a **market risk capital charge**, **graded NPA provisioning**, **ownership and governance rules**, **securitisation and debt restructuring**; **deregulated interest rates** and **premature withdrawal** conditions.

**Institutional and legal:** **Lok Adalats**, **debt recovery tribunals**, **asset reconstruction companies**, **SARFAESI Act 2002**, **CIBIL**, **CCIL** (central counterparty for fixed income and money market trades), the **Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code 2016**.

**Supervisory:** **Board for Financial Supervision** as apex body; **CAMELS rating**; **risk based supervision**; **consolidated supervision of conglomerates**; **off-site surveillance**; stronger **statutory audit and internal control**; **corporate governance and fit and proper tests**; the **EASE** programme (January 2018) for public sector banks.

**Technology:** **INFINET**, the **Negotiated Dealing System**, the **Payment and Settlement Systems Act 2007**, **RTGS, NEFT, ECS, ATMs, mobile and internet banking, IMPS and UPI**, plus **AI, machine learning, robotics, fintech tie-ups and blockchain**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Reserve requirements fell sharply, replaced by capital based discipline and market tools.

items.title: Reforms in monetary policy and in the money, government securities and capital markets
items.core_explanation_md:
**Monetary policy aims:** **price stability** and **adequate credit for productive sectors** to support growth. **Changes:** **broad money** was dropped as the intermediate target for a **multiple indicator approach**; **direct instruments** (**administered rates, reserve requirements, selective credit control**) gave way to **indirect instruments** (**open market operations**).

**Liquidity tools:**

- **Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF):** **repo and reverse repo auctions** form a **corridor** for the overnight rate and signal policy.
- **Standing Deposit Facility (SDF), 8 April 2022:** the **floor** of the policy corridor; the **Marginal Standing Facility (MSF)** is the **ceiling**.
- **Open market operations:** manage liquidity from **capital flows**.
- **Market Stabilization Scheme (MSS):** absorbs **enduring capital inflows** without disturbing LAF.

**Money market:** **interest rate deregulation** from the late **1980s**, **Commercial Paper and Certificates of Deposit**, **screen based trading**, **rupee swaps and forward rate agreements**, a wider **repo market**, and **tri-party repo** (**10 August 2017**, replacing **CBLO**).

**Government securities:** the **captive SLR market** gave way to **auctions**; **automatic monetisation** through **Ways and Means Advances** ended; since **April 2006** the Reserve Bank does **not** take part in the **primary market**.

**Capital market:** from the **Controller of Capital Issues** to **free pricing and book building**, **corporatised exchanges**, **screen trading**, **futures and options**, **rolling settlement replacing the 14-day cycle and Badla**, and **depositories**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A policy corridor with a floor (SDF) and ceiling (MSF) keeps the overnight rate within a band.

items.title: Reforms in the forex market
items.core_explanation_md:
**Before reform:** the market was **virtually non-existent**; exchange earners had to **surrender and buy foreign exchange from the Reserve Bank** at the **reference rate** and trades were **squared by day end**.

**Reform measures:** a **managed floating exchange rate**; a rationalised market structure; **new products** (**options, swaps**); a gradual shift to **capital account convertibility** with **Reserve Bank intervention** as needed.

**Liberalisation:** authorised dealers may **take trading positions** and **borrow and invest overseas** (with Board ratification); banks may set **interest rates on non-resident deposits** and use **derivatives for asset-liability management** within **open position and gap limits**; **exporters, Indians investing abroad and FIIs** may take **forward cover and swaps** against a **genuine underlying**; **FIIs and NRIs** may trade **exchange traded derivatives**; exporters may keep **foreign currency accounts (EEFC)**.

**Result:** a **market-based exchange rate**, **current account convertibility**, relaxed **capital account**, ability to **hold open positions** and **retain foreign exchange**, and **hedging tools**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Forex reforms moved the market from surrender-and-sell control to a market in which participants hedge and trade.

**Set up:** **December 2010** by the **Government of India**; **chaired by the Finance Minister**; **not a statutory body**.

**Purpose:** to **strengthen and institutionalise** the mechanism for **financial stability**, **financial sector development** and **inter-regulatory coordination**, avoiding **overlap** among **RBI, SEBI, IRDA and PFRDA**.

**Members:** **heads of RBI, SEBI, IRDAI and PFRDA**; the **Finance Secretary**; **Secretaries of DEA, DFS, Revenue and MeitY**; the **IBBI Chairman**; and the **Chief Economic Adviser**.

**Functions:** **financial stability and development**; **macro-prudential supervision** including **large financial conglomerates**; **inter-regulatory coordination**; **financial literacy and inclusion**.
